title: Semantic HTML and forms
runtime: Modern evergreen browser. HTML, CSS, and JavaScript fragments can be tried in a small local page or the browser DevTools described in the lesson.

objectives.text: Choose HTML elements for meaning before appearance.
Build a small form with labels, names, types, and native validation.
Explain button, link, and form submission behavior.

learningFlow: Apply it to a fresh page

diagnostic.question: What does HTML describe: appearance, document meaning, or both?
diagnostic.answer: HTML mainly describes content and structure. CSS controls most appearance.

sections.title: Semantic HTML gives content meaning
sections.body: Semantic elements describe the role of content. A nav contains major navigation, main contains the page’s primary content, and button performs an action. A div and span are neutral containers. Meaning helps browsers, assistive technology, search tools, developers, and tests understand the page.

sections.title: Build a clear document outline
sections.body: Use one main area for the unique page content. Use headings in a logical order that reflects sections, not for visual size. Header and footer describe their nearest section or the page. Article is useful for independently reusable content; section is useful when a titled grouping needs meaning.

sections.title: Links navigate; buttons act
sections.body: Use an anchor with href to move to a resource or page location. Use a button for actions such as Save, Open menu, or Add item. Native controls include keyboard behavior and platform semantics that a clickable div does not provide.

sections.title: A form sends named values
sections.body: A label tells the learner what an input expects. Match label for with input id. The name becomes the submitted field key. The type gives the browser useful behavior. A button inside a form submits by default, so write type="button" for a button that must not submit.

sections.title: Start with native constraints
sections.body: Attributes such as required, minlength, min, max, pattern, and a specific input type let the browser reject some invalid values. Client-side validation improves feedback but cannot protect a server; the server must validate untrusted input again.

sections.title: HTML meaning survives JSX
sections.body: React changes how you create elements, not what those elements mean. A React form still needs real labels, useful buttons, headings, and validation. Learn the native behavior before overriding it with event handlers.

examples.code:

Open the plan
examples.explanation: The article can stand on its own. Its heading names it, and the anchor navigates.
examples.tryThis: Replace the anchor with a button. Explain why that would change the meaning.

examples.title: A small native form
examples.code:
<form action="/subscribe" method="post">
  <label for="email">Email</label>
  <input id="email" name="email" type="email" required>
  <button type="submit">Subscribe</button>
</form>
examples.explanation: The label is associated with the input, the field has a submitted name, and the browser checks the email shape before normal submission.
examples.tryThis: Add a non-submit Preview button safely.

practice.prompt: Inside a form, what does <button>Preview</button> do by default?
hints: A button has a default type in a form.
acceptanceCriteria: Explain the evidence or rule behind the answer.
Complete the attempt before opening the solution.

solution.explanation: It acts as type="submit". Use type="button" when Preview must not submit.

practice.prompt: Write a search form with a label, a named search input, and a submit button.
hints: Use type="search" and connect for to id.
acceptanceCriteria: Explain the evidence or rule behind the answer.
Complete the attempt before opening the solution.

solution.explanation: One valid solution is shown. Other solutions are acceptable when they meet the criteria and preserve the same behavior.
solution.code: <form action="/search"><label for="query">Search</label><input id="query" name="q" type="search" required><button type="submit">Search</button></form>

practice.prompt: An input has id="email" but its label has for="user-email". Explain the bug and fix it.
hints: The two values must match exactly.
acceptanceCriteria: Explain the evidence or rule behind the answer.
Complete the attempt before opening the solution.

solution.explanation: Change the label to for="email" or change the input id to user-email. The association then supports focus and assistive technology.

practice.prompt: Choose elements for a site title, primary navigation, page content, save action, and privacy-page navigation.
acceptanceCriteria: Explain the evidence or rule behind the answer.
Complete the attempt before opening the solution.

solution.explanation: Use a heading in header, nav for major links, main for unique content, button for Save, and an anchor with href for the Privacy page.

practice.prompt: Design a delivery form with address, delivery speed, and optional instructions. State which fields need labels, names, grouping, and validation.
hints: Related radio buttons share a name and benefit from fieldset and legend.
acceptanceCriteria: Explain the evidence or rule behind the answer.
Complete the attempt before opening the solution.

solution.explanation: Give every control a label and name. Group delivery-speed radios in fieldset with legend and one shared name. Mark only required business fields required. Use textarea for instructions and validate again on the server.

interviewQuestions.question: Why does semantic HTML matter in a React application?
interviewQuestions.answer: React still produces HTML. Correct elements provide meaning, keyboard behavior, accessibility hooks, clearer code, and more reliable tests.

interviewQuestions.question: When should you use a link instead of a button?
interviewQuestions.answer: Use a link for navigation to a URL or document location. Use a button for an action in the current interface.
interviewQuestions.followUp: How should a link that looks like a button be implemented?

interviewQuestions.question: Is client-side form validation enough?
interviewQuestions.answer: No. It improves user feedback, but requests can bypass the browser. The server must validate all untrusted values.
interviewQuestions.followUp: Which native constraints would you try before JavaScript?

mastery.policy: Reading the lesson or revealing help is not mastery. Save an attempt first, then prove the idea again without the solution and use it in a fresh situation.

checks.evidence: Explain semantic html and forms without copying the lesson.
checks.pass: The explanation uses correct terms and gives one practical reason.

checks.evidence: Complete at least four practice tasks before revealing their solutions.
checks.pass: The saved work meets each acceptance criterion and explains the reasoning.

checks.evidence: Use the lesson in a new small page or debugging case.
checks.pass: The new example works and the learner can explain one decision and one tradeoff.

reviewSchedule.note: Complete these without reopening the lesson. Compare only after saving an answer.

problems.prompt: Write the three most useful rules from Semantic HTML and forms.
problems.solution: A good answer states three accurate rules, explains why each matters, and uses at least one concrete example.

problems.prompt: Describe one common semantic html and forms mistake and repair it.
problems.solution: Choose one mistake from the lesson, identify its cause, and apply the smallest fix that preserves correct web behavior.

problems.prompt: Teach semantic html and forms to a beginner in five sentences.
problems.solution: The explanation should define the idea, show how it works, give a real use, warn about a mistake, and name a way to test it.

problems.prompt: Create a different example from the lesson and explain how you verified it.
problems.solution: The example must use the same core concept in a new context and name observable evidence from the browser or code.

commonMistakes.symptom: A clickable div cannot be reached or activated by keyboard
commonMistakes.cause: The div has no native button behavior.
commonMistakes.fix: Use button for an action. Style the button instead of rebuilding its semantics.

commonMistakes.symptom: Clicking a form button reloads or submits unexpectedly
commonMistakes.cause: A button inside a form defaults to submit.
commonMistakes.fix: Choose type="submit" intentionally or set type="button" for other actions.

commonMistakes.symptom: A visible word sits near an input but is not announced as its label
commonMistakes.cause: Visual proximity does not create a programmatic relationship.
commonMistakes.fix: Use label for matching the input id, or a valid implicit label.
